entries.review_description: Drawing canvas. The blank drawing surface and its resting canvas chrome. Captured in light mode on iPhone 13 mini in portrait at 375 × 812. Assess visible hierarchy, spacing, text fit, clipping, overlap, touch-target clarity, modal scrolling, and visual consistency. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

Report has transparent tap padding beyond its visible label; it does not need a separate filled button. The visibility floor is readable disclosure and Report text, with a distinguishable flag against the pill.
entries.critique: The disclosure and Report text are readable against the dark pill, and the flag is distinguishable. The Download label and close glyph are also clear in night mode.

entries.review_description: AI result · report confirmation. The confirmation and retention notice before a report is sent. Captured in light mode on iPhone 13 mini in portrait at 375 × 812. Assess visible hierarchy, spacing, text fit, clipping, overlap, touch-target clarity, modal scrolling, and visual consistency. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

entries.review_description: Beta sign-up · Android. Google Play closed-test instructions in the Android panel of the beta page. Captured in light mode on iPhone 16 Pro Max in portrait at 440 × 956. Assess visible hierarchy, spacing, text fit, clipping, overlap, touch-target clarity, modal scrolling, and visual consistency. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

entries.review_description: Settings · Coloring. The Coloring section where full settings fit; compact phone landscapes show the quick-toggle shell that replaces it. Design intent: When this image shows the compact phone-landscape Settings shell, its Portrait and Landscape orientation segments are both inactive while screen rotation is unlocked. A segment becomes active only after the parent locks rotation to that orientation. Captured in night mode on iPad Pro 13-inch (M4) in portrait at 1032 × 1376. Assess only night-mode contrast and legibility. Ignore layout and responsive composition. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

In portrait it is the column of drawing controls near the lower left; in landscape it is the row along the bottom. entries.review_description: Coloring-book picker. The installed coloring-book cover grid. Captured in light mode on iPad Pro 13-inch (M4) in portrait at 1032 × 1376. Assess visible hierarchy, spacing, text fit, clipping, overlap, touch-target clarity, modal scrolling, and visual consistency. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.
entries.surface_description: The installed coloring-book cover grid.
entries.critique: Clear title and orderly two-column grid with consistent card sizes, spacing, and artwork treatment. All eight covers and labels fit without clipping or overlap. Cards and close control have clear touch targets. The full grid fits within the modal, with comfortable bottom padding and no visible scrolling issue. The scrim consistently dims the surrounding page.

entries.review_description: Settings · Feedback. The Feedback section where full settings fit; compact phone landscapes show the quick-toggle shell that replaces it. Design intent: When this image shows the compact phone-landscape Settings shell, its Portrait and Landscape orientation segments are both inactive while screen rotation is unlocked. A segment becomes active only after the parent locks rotation to that orientation. When this image shows the Feedback form, the "Send report" button stays disabled until the message box has text, and the form is captured before anything has been typed, so that button is in its disabled state here. A disabled button is drawn at half opacity, fill and label together, which is how this app marks the action unavailable; that half-strength appearance is the disabled styling arriving and is not a claim about the button’s contrast once a message is typed and it is enabled. The floor it still owes is that its label remains readable: report it only when you cannot read the words "Send report" on it. Captured in night mode on iPhone 13 mini in landscape at 812 × 375. Assess only night-mode contrast and legibility. Ignore layout and responsive composition. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

entries.review_description: Drawing canvas. The blank drawing surface and its resting canvas chrome. Captured in light mode on iPhone 16 Pro Max in landscape at 956 × 440. Assess visible hierarchy, spacing, text fit, clipping, overlap, touch-target clarity, modal scrolling, and visual consistency. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. entries.review_description: Settings · overview. The phone section hub and tablet split-pane default view. Design intent: When this image shows the compact phone-landscape Settings shell, its Portrait and Landscape orientation segments are both inactive while screen rotation is unlocked. A segment becomes active only after the parent locks rotation to that orientation. Captured in night mode on iPad mini 7th Gen (2024) in landscape at 1133 × 744. Assess only night-mode contrast and legibility. Ignore layout and responsive composition. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

entries.review_description: Install banner · instructions. The expanded iOS Share-sheet guidance. Captured in light mode on iPad mini 7th Gen (2024) in landscape at 1133 × 744. Assess visible hierarchy, spacing, text fit, clipping, overlap, touch-target clarity, modal scrolling, and visual consistency. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

entries.review_description: AI result · server error. The generic generation failure treatment. Captured in light mode on iPad mini 7th Gen (2024) in landscape at 1133 × 744. Assess visible hierarchy, spacing, text fit, clipping, overlap, touch-target clarity, modal scrolling, and visual consistency. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

entries.review_description: Clear gesture · threshold. The accept ring and paper wash while held past threshold. Design intent: The faint icons washed over the canvas are the intended effect: they signal that clearing the drawing is underway. While the round trash button is being dragged, the accept ring stays centered on the button’s docked position at the screen edge. The ring may extend beyond the viewport; at least one arc of the ring remains visible. Captured in night mode on iPad Pro 13-inch (M4) in landscape at 1376 × 1032. Assess only night-mode contrast and legibility. Ignore layout and responsive composition. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence. Use severity pass, low, medium, or high. A pass means there is no actionable visible issue and requires a null recommendation; otherwise give one specific recommendation. Return concise issue-category tags.

entries.review_description: Admin · access-code actions. The in-place row expansion on phones and inline actions on tablets. Captured in light mode on iPad Pro 13-inch (M4) in landscape at 1376 × 1032. Assess visible hierarchy, spacing, text fit, clipping, overlap, touch-target clarity, modal scrolling, and visual consistency. Design decisions already settled for this app, given as context for what you are looking at rather than as a judgement of it: The round trash button that clears the drawing is docked against the edge of the screen on purpose, with part of it deliberately past the edge; it is not being clipped or cut off by the viewport. Pressing it undocks it. The chevron that expands and collapses the bottom-corner button panel, and the settings button in the opposite bottom corner, are drawn as thin low-contrast gray glyphs with no filled button, disc, or outline behind them, so they sit back from the child’s artwork; they are the parent-facing controls on this screen, and a child who never notices them is the point. Seeing them read as quiet, subdued, faint, easy to overlook at a glance, or much weaker than the drawing tools is that styling arriving, in either theme, and is the resting appearance of those two controls rather than a contrast finding about them. The floor they still owe is that the glyph remains findable: report one only when you cannot locate its shape anywhere in this image. Where a scrolling region continues past its edge, this app marks it with a soft gradient fade along that edge, and deliberately ships no arrow, scrollbar, or second indicator beside it. The fade is painted over the last line, row, or card rather than beside it, so that content thins out toward the edge and can read as blurred, smeared, washed out, grayed, or half-erased. That thinning is the cue itself being drawn — not a rendering artifact, a focus or compression fault, or a legibility problem in the region — so judge a scrolling region on the content that sits clear of its faded strip. Several overlays here are dialogs that lay a scrim over the whole page behind them — the settings card, the color picker, the coloring-book and AI cards, the parent gate. Each open card lays one sheet with nothing above it but the card itself: the sheet darkens (and on most cards also blurs) the canvas, the strip of color swatches along the top edge (the left edge in landscape), the docked trash button, the bottom-corner button panel, and the corner glyphs all at once, in both themes, so the open card holds attention. When a second card opens over the first, the first card sits under the second card’s sheet and is out of scope; the card to judge is the front card — the one no sheet is drawn over. The swatches and the trash button are saturated colors, so under the sheet they still read as colored while the paper reads gray, and the swatch strip keeps its own crisp edge against the paper; a band of color or a hard seam there is those elements showing through the same sheet as everything else, not a gap in it or a layer it missed. The floor a scrim owes is that it darkens everything outside the front card: report its coverage only when a region outside that card shows no darkening at all — in light mode a white strip still white or paper still bright, in night mode the strip’s own background between the swatches, or the paper, no darker than the card’s own surface — rather than when it looks brighter than the paper beside it. Where you can see that the page behind an overlay has been darkened that way, background content reading dim, gray, soft, or blurred is that scrim rather than the styling of the elements beneath it, and the contrast and legibility to judge are those of the front card — its text, its controls, its close button — together with anything drawn on top of its sheet. The brush and stroke-width flyouts cast no scrim: where the page behind an overlay is still at full brightness, every element in the frame keeps its usual scope. In the bottom-corner panel of round buttons (the Actions Panel), the undo, AI, and screenshot buttons are drawn at reduced contrast whenever they are disabled, which is how this app marks them unavailable until at least one stroke is on the canvas. That reduced contrast is intended for those three buttons while they are in that disabled state; it is not a claim about their contrast once they are enabled. Judge only visible evidence.
